blocks.text: Have you ever wondered why ice melts into water or how rain forms from clouds? Let's explore the states of matter and their transformations!

blocks.markdown: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Everything around us is made up of matter, which exists in three primary states: solids, liquids, and gases.

blocks.title: States of Matter
blocks.text: The three states of matter are solids, liquids, and gases. Each has distinct characteristics based on the arrangement of its particles.

blocks.markdown: In solids, particles are tightly packed in a fixed arrangement, giving them a definite shape and volume. Examples include a table or a rock. In liquids, particles are close but can move past each other, allowing liquids to flow and take the shape of their container, like water in a cup. Gases have particles that are far apart and move freely, filling any available space, such as the air we breathe.

blocks.title: Understanding Changes of State
blocks.prompt: Let's consider how water changes state.

steps.text: Start with ice, a solid. As it absorbs heat, it melts into water, a liquid.
When water is heated further, it evaporates into steam, a gas.
Conversely, when steam cools, it condenses back into water, and when water is cooled further, it freezes back into ice.

blocks.answer: This cycle demonstrates the processes of melting, evaporation, condensation, and freezing.

blocks.markdown: In Nigeria, you can observe these states of matter in everyday life. Ice blocks sold by vendors are solids, palm oil in bottles is a liquid, and the steam from cooking rice is a gas.

blocks.title: Exam Tip
blocks.text: Remember, the key to understanding matter is how particles are arranged and move in each state. This will help you in exams when explaining properties or changes of state.

points: Matter exists in three states: solid, liquid, and gas.
The arrangement and movement of particles determine the state of matter.
Everyday examples include ice (solid), water (liquid), and steam (gas).
Processes like melting and evaporation involve changes between these states.
